title: The Frame-Maker's Son: Birmingham, Exeter College, and the Long Sleep at Avalon
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Birmingham, the birth near Bennett's Hill
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date. The pin is an approximation from the cathedral source's remark that he was born and baptised near Bennett's Hill; the frame-maker's exact address was not established this session.
stops.campa: In a frame-maker's house near Bennett's Hill, Birmingham, a son is born and named Edward Coley Burne Jones, the surname not yet hyphenated. Days later his mother is dead, and the boy will know her only as an absence in a quiet house. No source consulted names her. The father, by his son's later account, is a poetical little fellow, tender-hearted and touching, quite unfit for the world into which he was pitched. There is no other child in the house and no visitor the boy afterwards recalls except a neighbouring garden. What fills the rooms instead of company is paper.
stops.quote: I was always drawing. Unmothered, with a sad papa, without sister or brother, always alone, I was never unhappy, because I was always drawing.
stops.quote_source: Edward Burne-Jones, his own words recorded by a friend and quoted in Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones, Vol. I, Ch. I (London: Macmillan, 1904)
suggested_refs: Bennett's Hill and the streets of the frame-making trade in 1830s Birmingham
sources: Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones, Vol. I, Chs. I-II

stops.name: King Edward's School, Birmingham, the Commercial side
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1844; no month is given in the sources consulted, so the day defaults.
stops.campa: At eleven he enters King Edward VI grammar school in Birmingham, a free school of the town's own making, and passes out of the frame-maker's rooms into a hall of boys. He is put first into the Commercial School, where the sons of tradesmen are taught the arithmetic of trade. The Classical School, with its Latin and its Greek and its road to the universities, sits on the other side of the building. He will cross to it, and a boy already there will remember the day he did. Meanwhile he draws in the margin of everything the school puts in front of him.
suggested_refs: King Edward VI Grammar School, New Street, Birmingham, and its division between Commercial and Classical schools
sources: Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials, Vol. I, Ch. III

stops.name: Birmingham School of Art, the evening classes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1848; no month is given, so the day defaults.
stops.campa: At fifteen he begins at the Birmingham School of Art, in a manufacturing town that has built a school of design because its trades need designers: japanners, jewellers, glass-cutters, men who put ornament on metal. He is learning the drawing his father's trade framed and never made. The school was founded for the workshops and not for any academy, and thirteen years from now William Morris will offer him the same arrangement in the form of a firm with a prospectus and a ledger. He does not yet know Morris exists.
suggested_refs: The Birmingham School of Art and the government schools of design founded for the manufacturing towns

stops.name: King Edward's School, crossing into the Classical
stops.date_confidence: Dixon's recollection places the crossing at about fifteen, and the chapter that carries it is headed 1849-1851. The year is a reasonable fix within that span, not a documented date.
stops.campa: He crosses into the Classical School, tall for his age and looking it. Richard Watson Dixon, later a canon and a poet, is sitting among the younger boys when the newcomer takes his desk, and remembers the entrance for fifty years. Cormell Price remembers something else first: the laugh, before he knew him any other way. The Birmingham boys who gather round him here will follow him to Oxford and become the nucleus of a brotherhood none of them has yet thought of. A schoolfellow watches him fill a sheet of foolscap as fast as a man could write.
stops.quote: I first saw E. B.-J. when he came into the Classical from the Commercial School. He would then be about fifteen. He was a tall, strong boy, and I remember noticing his appearance as he sat proud and erect at his desk among the somewhat younger boys of that class.
stops.quote_source: Canon Richard Watson Dixon, quoted in Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones, Vol. I, Ch. III
suggested_refs: The Birmingham Set: Burne-Jones, Dixon, Cormell Price and their schoolfellows
sources: Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials, Vol. I, Ch. III

stops.name: King Edward's School, the young priest before the altar
stops.date_confidence: the source dates the drawing only to c. 1849-1851, the span of Memorials Vol. I, Ch. III. The pin at 1850 is the mid-point of that span and is not a documented date.
stops.campa: Among the sheets he covers at school is a young priest standing before an altar, drawn as carefully as the mountains he puts behind everything although he has never seen a mountain. He shows it to Dixon and says what he means by it. He is bound for the Church; the drawing is a plan and not a picture. In 1853 he will go up to Oxford to read theology with ordination in view, and by 1856 the plan will be gone. The altars and the vestments stay. He goes on drawing them for another forty-eight years, in oil and in glass, for churches he does not serve.
stops.quote: That is what I hope to be one day.
stops.quote_source: Edward Burne-Jones to R. W. Dixon, c. 1849-1851, quoted in Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones, Vol. I, Ch. III
suggested_refs: The schoolboy drawings of clergy and altars preserved in the Memorials
sources: Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials, Vol. I, Chs. I and III

stops.name: Exeter College, Oxford, the meeting with Morris
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of entry, 1853. The atlas's william_morris.journey.json places the meeting on his first day and supplies this pin; no calendar date for the meeting is documented, so the day defaults.
stops.campa: He goes up to Exeter College, Oxford, to read theology, meaning to be ordained. He meets William Morris there, another intending clergyman, and the two recognise each other at once. The friendship runs forty years and outlives the vocation that brought each of them here. Within three years both have turned from the Church toward the Middle Age as a matter of art. Morris will build the workshops; Burne-Jones will draw the figures that go into them. Neither man takes holy orders. Both spend their working lives on churches all the same.
stops.quote: I think Morris's friendship began everything for me; everything that I afterwards cared for; we were freshmen together at Exeter. When I left Oxford I got to know Rossetti, whose friendship I sought and obtained. He is, you know, the most generous of men to the young. I couldn't bear with a young man's dreadful sensitiveness and conceit as he bore with mine. He taught me practically all I ever learnt; afterwards I made a method for myself to suit my nature.
stops.quote_source: Edward Burne-Jones in conversation, recorded in J. Comyns Carr, Coasting Bohemia (Project Gutenberg ebook #66838)
suggested_refs: Exeter College, Oxford, and the Oxford theology curriculum of the 1850s
sources: william_morris.journey.json, stop 'Exeter College, Oxford, the meeting with Burne-Jones'

stops.name: Oxford, The Nature of Gothic read aloud
stops.date_confidence: contested between two canonical atlas files and not adjudicated here: william_morris.journey.json gives the Oxford reading as a span, 1853-1856; marcel_proust.journey.json, citing that same file, dates it 1856. Pinned at the opening of the span.
stops.campa: Morris reads aloud from Ruskin's The Nature of Gothic, the chapter of The Stones of Venice which argues that a building is worth what the hands that cut it were free to be. The two undergraduates take it as doctrine. They read Tennyson and Malory beside it and walk the Oxford churches with it in mind. Fifty years on, Marcel Proust will translate Ruskin into French; in 1904 Gandhi will read Unto This Last on a night train in Natal and go off to found a settlement. Morris reprints the chapter at his own press before he dies.
suggested_refs: John Ruskin, 'The Nature of Gothic', The Stones of Venice, vol. II (1853), later reprinted by the Kelmscott Press
sources: william_morris.journey.json, stops 'Exeter College' and 'The Nature of Gothic, Ruskin read at Oxford'
marcel_proust.journey.json, stop 'The Ruskin translation appears with a long preface'

stops.name: Oxford, Malory and Rossetti turn him from the Church
stops.date_confidence: [R] reconstruction. The research pool tags the shift as general biographical consensus with no firmly documented date; 1855 is the conventional placing, not an attestation.
stops.campa: Somewhere in these Oxford years the plan of ordination gives way. He finds Dante Gabriel Rossetti's work and Malory's Morte d'Arthur in the same season, and the second confirms what the first proposes: that the Middle Age can be entered through paint and need not be preached. Rossetti himself he has not yet met, and will not until he has left Oxford. The Arthurian material he takes up now holds him for forty-three years, from the Oxford Union walls to the unfinished Avalon on his easel the week he dies.
suggested_refs: Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, in the Southey edition read at Oxford
lancelot.journey.json and guinevere.journey.json, on the Pre-Raphaelite Arthurian tradition

stops.name: Oxford, the Brotherhood and the leaving
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1856 for all four events, and deliberately not back-dated: the research pool's original chronology placed the Brotherhood in 1853, which the verification pass rejected. No months are documented, so the day defaults.
stops.campa: With Morris and the Birmingham men he forms the society they call the Brotherhood: a half-earnest vow of crusade against the age, conducted through reading, church-crawling, and a magazine. The name belongs to this year and not to their arrival three years earlier. In the same twelvemonth he makes his first sketch in oils, becomes engaged to Georgiana MacDonald, and leaves Oxford without taking a degree, on Rossetti's encouragement, for London and no visible income. He is twenty-three and has been trained for a profession he has just refused.
suggested_refs: The Oxford and Cambridge Magazine (1856), organ of the Brotherhood

segments.name: Red Lion Square, the Union Wall, and Italy

stops.name: 17 Red Lion Square, London, rooms with Morris
stops.date_confidence: date and pin inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json, stop 'Street's office and Red Lion Square'.
stops.campa: Morris quits Street's architectural office and takes rooms with Burne-Jones at 17 Red Lion Square in Bloomsbury. Two young men, one with private means and one with none, keep house together, build their own furniture because nothing sold in London will do, and then paint it. Rossetti comes and goes without any arrangement to teach either of them. Burne-Jones will say afterwards that Rossetti taught him practically all he ever learnt, and that he then made a method for himself to suit his own nature.
suggested_refs: 17 Red Lion Square, the painted furniture made by Morris and Burne-Jones for their own rooms
sources: william_morris.journey.json, stop 'Street's office and Red Lion Square'

stops.name: Oxford Union, the Arthurian murals
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1857; the summer month is conventional and the pool gives no date within the year.
stops.campa: Rossetti gathers a crew of amateurs to paint the Arthurian legend onto the new debating hall of the Oxford Union, and Burne-Jones joins it. They work in distemper on damp brick that has not been prepared to take paint; within a few years the pictures begin to sink into the wall and become ghosts of themselves. Not one of the painters has been taught to prepare a surface. He has found the material he will spend his life on, in a room where the material is already fading off the plaster.
suggested_refs: The Oxford Union murals of 1857 and their early deterioration

stops.name: Florence, the first journey to Italy
stops.date_confidence: the year is corrected: the research pool originally gave 1857, which the verification pass rejected as wrong by two years, a collision with the Oxford Union murals. The source reads 1859. No month is attested for any leg, so the month here is arbitrary and the city order follows the source's own list.
stops.campa: He crosses to Italy for the first time and reaches Florence: Botticelli, Fra Angelico, the early men who painted before the High Renaissance made painting easy. He looks at line and at pattern rather than at bravura, and takes home what the Pre-Raphaelites in London had guessed at from engravings. Pisa and Siena follow on the same journey. Morris will go north instead, in later years, to Iceland and the sagas; the two friends divide the map of the past between them, and quarrel about the division for the rest of their lives.
stops.quote: I quarrel now with Morris about Art. He journeys to Iceland, and I to Italy, which is a symbol, and I quarrel, too, with Rossetti. If I could travel backwards I think my heart's desire would take me to Florence in the time of Botticelli.
stops.quote_source: Edward Burne-Jones in conversation, recorded in J. Comyns Carr, Coasting Bohemia (undated)
suggested_refs: The Uffizi and the Florentine quattrocento as Burne-Jones saw it in 1859

stops.name: Venice, the last of the Italian cities
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested and corrected from the pool's erroneous 1857. Venice is last in the source's list of cities; whether the list is an itinerary is not stated, and the month is arbitrary.
stops.campa: The journey ends at Venice, the city Ruskin had anatomised stone by stone in the book Morris read aloud at Oxford. Burne-Jones sees the mosaics, the Bellinis, the gold grounds. Florence, Pisa, Siena and Venice stand in that order in the only list of the journey the sources give, and whether the list is a route nobody says. He comes home to London with a set of standards no English exhibition can meet, and paints from the four hundred years before Raphael rather than the four hundred after. He is twenty-six, unexhibited, and engaged to be married.
suggested_refs: John Ruskin, The Stones of Venice, against which the 1859 journey can be read

stops.name: Red House, Bexleyheath, the murals for Morris
stops.date_confidence: date and pin inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json, stop 'Red House, Bexleyheath, the medieval dream made a home'.
stops.campa: Morris, married the year before, has had Philip Webb build him a red-brick house at Bexleyheath, and the friends come out from London to decorate it: embroidery on the walls, painted furniture, a ceiling done by hand. Burne-Jones paints murals there, scenes out of romance on the plaster of a private house. Georgiana records her husband's verdict on the place in his own words. It is the first house the group decorates together. Within ten months the same men will be constituted as a company with a prospectus and seven partners.
stops.quote_source: Edward Burne-Jones on Red House, recorded by Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones, and cited at the Red House stop of william_morris.journey.json
suggested_refs: Red House, Bexleyheath, built by Philip Webb, and the surviving traces of the Burne-Jones murals
sources: william_morris.journey.json, stop 'Red House, Bexleyheath, the medieval dream made a home'

stops.name: Manchester, the marriage to Georgiana MacDonald
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 9 June 1860. The town is attested: Wikipedia, 'Georgiana Burne-Jones', 'Georgiana and Edward married in Manchester on 9 June 1860'. The pin is the centre of Manchester and must not be read as the church, which no source consulted names. It replaces the default London coordinate carried by the research pool, which put the wedding some 260 km from the city where it happened.
stops.campa: He marries Georgiana MacDonald, four years after the engagement and one week after the summer at Red House. She is one of the MacDonald sisters, out of a Methodist manse; through her sisters the family acquires within a generation a Prime Minister for a nephew and Rudyard Kipling for a nephew by marriage. In the same year he draws Sidonia von Bork and Clara von Bork, two watercolours of a sorceress and her opposite. Georgiana outlives him by decades and writes the book from which most of this journey is quarried.
suggested_refs: The MacDonald sisters and their marriages into the Burne-Jones, Kipling, Poynter and Baldwin families
sources: Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones (1904)

stops.name: 8 Red Lion Square, the prospectus of the Firm
stops.date_confidence: date and pin inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json, stop '8 Red Lion Square, the founding of the Firm'.
stops.campa: The prospectus goes out from 8 Red Lion Square on the eleventh of April: Morris, Marshall, Faulkner and Company, Fine Art Workmen in Painting, Carving, Furniture and the Metals. The partners are Morris, Ford Madox Brown, Charles Faulkner, Rossetti, P. P. Marshall, Philip Webb, and Burne-Jones, who has no capital and supplies figures instead. In the same year his son Philip is born. He is twenty-eight. He has exhibited almost nothing and is now a partner in a manufacturing company.
suggested_refs: The 1861 prospectus of Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co.
sources: william_morris.journey.json, stop '8 Red Lion Square, the founding of the Firm'

stops.name: London, the cartoons for the leaded saints
stops.date_confidence: 1862 is attested for the Tristram and Isoude panels and for the International Exhibition. The pin is inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json, whose stained-glass stop carries the place string 'Oxford / England (churches)' against a Bloomsbury coordinate; this stop is named for the London drawing office so that pin and prose agree. The mismatch inside the Morris file is flagged, not repaired.
stops.campa: In the drawing office the division of labour settles into what it will remain for thirty-five years: Burne-Jones draws the figures, Morris leads the colour and the ornament. He designs the Tristram and Isoude panels this year, and after them angels, saints, kings out of legend, cartoons by the hundred that leave London as paper and arrive at Jesus College and Christ Church in Oxford, and in parish churches across England, as leaded light. The Firm's showing at the London International Exhibition makes its name.
suggested_refs: The Tristram and Isoude stained-glass panels (1862)
Morris & Co. windows at Jesus College and Christ Church, Oxford
sources: william_morris.journey.json, stop 'The stained glass, light through leaded saints'

stops.name: Pall Mall East, the Water-Colour Society and The Merciful Knight
stops.date_confidence: the picture is conventionally dated 1863 and the exhibition is attested for 1864; the pool's standalone 1863 entry was rejected by the verification pass because the cited source anchors the event to 1864. The two are merged here and the day defaults.
stops.campa: He is elected an associate of the Society of Painters in Water-Colours and exhibits, among other works, The Merciful Knight: a knight embracing a crucifix whose carved Christ leans down from the wood to return the embrace. The subject is a legend of forgiveness granted to a man who spared his enemy. It is the first picture in which the whole later manner is present, the frozen gesture, the crowded flowers, the faces that do not look out. Critics find it morbid. He has six years of public exhibiting left.
suggested_refs: The Merciful Knight (1863), Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery

stops.name: Great Russell Street, the scarlet fever and the death of Christopher
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1864; no month is given for the illness or for the birth and death of the child, so the month here is arbitrary. The street is attested: Wikipedia, 'Georgiana Burne-Jones', places the couple in rented rooms in Great Russell Street from the marriage until the move to 41 Kensington Square that followed this loss. No house number is given in the sources consulted, so the pin is the middle of the street and not a doorway. It replaces the default Charing Cross coordinate carried by the research pool.
stops.campa: Georgiana takes scarlet fever and nearly dies of it. A son, Christopher, is born during the illness and lives only briefly. Burne-Jones nurses her and goes on working, and says little of it in the record his wife later assembled. The same twelve months bring him his election to the Water-Colour Society and his first professional standing. The house holds two surviving children, Philip, and, two years on, Margaret. No source consulted gives the month of the child's birth or of his death.
suggested_refs: Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials, Vol. I, on the illness of 1864

segments.name: Kensington, Fulham, and the Years Out of Sight

stops.name: 41 Kensington Square, Margaret born and Maria Zambaco
stops.date_confidence: 1866 is attested both for Margaret's birth at 41 Kensington Square and for the beginning of the affair; no months are given, so the day defaults. The pin is the attested address of the birth, not of the affair.
stops.campa: Margaret is born at 41 Kensington Square. In the same year her father begins an affair with Maria Zambaco, a Greek-born artist who is his pupil and his model, and the affair becomes known across artistic London. It nearly ends the marriage. Georgiana stays. Zambaco's face, heavy-lidded and long-necked, enters the pictures and does not leave them; she is the Nimue who seals Merlin under the stone in the painting he works at through these years, and the Phyllis who bursts from the almond tree in the picture that ends his exhibiting.
suggested_refs: Maria Zambaco, sculptor and medallist of the Greek colony in London, as model for Nimue and for Phyllis

stops.name: South Kensington Museum, the Green Dining Room
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1867; no month is given, so the day defaults.
stops.campa: For the Firm he designs the decoration of the Green Dining Room at the South Kensington Museum: panelled walls, painted figures, stained glass in the upper lights. It is a public commission in a national museum, given to a company six years old whose partners had begun by making their own chairs at Red Lion Square because nothing sold in London would do. The division of labour is the one settled in the glass: he draws the figures, Morris takes the pattern and the colour. The room survives, still in use, in the building that becomes the Victoria and Albert.
suggested_refs: The Green Dining Room (Morris Room), Victoria and Albert Museum, South Kensington

stops.name: The Grange, North End, Fulham, the house for the rest of his life
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1867; no month is given. The coordinate is the corrected Fulham location of the Grange, replacing the generic London pin carried in the research pool.
stops.campa: The family moves to the Grange in North End, Fulham, an eighteenth-century house at the western edge of London with a garden and a long studio. He lives and works here for thirty-one years and dies in it. The house takes in Sunday breakfasts, nephews, and William Morris week after week for decades. Unfinished canvases stand against the studio wall, some of them for twenty years before anyone outside is shown them. The address becomes half of his title when the baronetcy comes.
suggested_refs: The Grange, North End Road, Fulham, demolished in the twentieth century

stops.name: The Grange, the first Pygmalion
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1868 as the beginning of the first series, completed over the following two years; no month is given.
stops.campa: He begins the first Pygmalion series, four panels telling the sculptor's story in sequence: the heart desires, the hand refrains, the godhead fires, the soul attains. A man makes a woman out of stone and is granted her as flesh. He paints it in the years of the Zambaco affair, and he will paint the four subjects again in the years after. The work is done at the Grange behind a closed door, on canvases the public will not see for a decade. Nothing of it is offered to a gallery while it is being made.
stops.quote: I thank the Lord in heaven that he gave me a savage passion for work.
stops.quote_source: Edward Burne-Jones, quoted in Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones, Vol. II, Ch. XVI (1868-1871), undated within the chapter
suggested_refs: The two Pygmalion and the Image series, Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery
sources: Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials, Vol. II, Ch. XVI

stops.name: Pall Mall East, Phyllis and Demophoon and the resignation
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1870 for the controversy, the resignation, and the start of the withdrawal; no month is given, so the day defaults.
stops.campa: He shows Phyllis and Demophoon at the Society of Painters in Water-Colours: Phyllis, turned into an almond tree by grief, bursting out of the trunk to seize the lover who abandoned her, and Demophoon naked and recoiling. The Society objects to the nudity of the male figure. He is asked to alter it, declines, and resigns his associateship. For roughly seven years afterwards he shows almost nothing in public. In those years he paints The Beguiling of Merlin and Pan and Psyche, and exhibits neither.
stops.quote: I want big things to do and vast spaces, and for common people to see them and say Oh! -- only Oh!
stops.quote_source: Edward Burne-Jones, a recurring saying reported in Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones, Vol. II, Ch. XVI, undated
suggested_refs: Phyllis and Demophoon (1870), Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery
sources: Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials, Vol. II, Ch. XVI

stops.name: Red Lion Square, the Firm dissolved
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The pin is the Firm's founding address, inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json; the dissolution was a legal act rather than an event at a stated place.
stops.campa: The Firm is dissolved on the last day of March amid a dispute among the partners over what each is owed for his share, and is reconstituted under Morris's sole ownership as Morris and Company. Rossetti and Madox Brown take settlements and go; Burne-Jones and Webb take nothing and stay, working for Morris as before. He goes on drawing the figures for another twenty-one years, down to the last book Morris ever prints. Georgiana, writing it up thirty years later, gives the friendship a sentence of her own that has been quoted as his ever since.
stops.quote: Nothing ever interrupted the intimacy with Morris; that friendship was like one of the forces of nature.
stops.quote_source: Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones, Vol. II, Ch. XVI: her own authorial comment, not a Burne-Jones utterance, and undated
suggested_refs: The 1875 dissolution deed and the reconstitution as Morris & Co.

stops.name: Grosvenor Gallery, New Bond Street, the eight oils
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month, May 1877, for the gallery's opening exhibition and for the first showing of The Beguiling of Merlin; the day defaults.
stops.campa: The Grosvenor Gallery opens on New Bond Street as a rival to the Royal Academy, hanging pictures the Academy will not take, and Burne-Jones sends eight oils to the first exhibition. Among them is The Beguiling of Merlin, five years on the easel: Nimue reading the book of spells over the enchanter she is sealing under a hawthorn, and Merlin already half wood. He is forty-three and has shown almost nothing in public for seven years. The reviews of the opening make him the most discussed painter in England.
suggested_refs: The Beguiling of Merlin (1872-1877), Lady Lever Art Gallery, Port Sunlight

stops.name: Grosvenor Gallery, Laus Veneris and the Chant d'Amour
stops.date_confidence: 1878 is attested for the exhibition of Laus Veneris, Chant d'Amour and Pan and Psyche. The research pool originally placed The Annunciation and the second Pygmalion series here; the verification pass rejected both, dating The Annunciation to the 1879 Grosvenor exhibition and the second Pygmalion series to 1875-78.
stops.campa: He shows Laus Veneris, the Chant d'Amour and Pan and Psyche at the Grosvenor. The Venus of Laus Veneris sits burning in a red gown among women who are not looking at her, in a room with no visible exit; the title is Swinburne's. The pictures are bought, argued over and engraved, and the engravings go abroad. Within a few years his work is being copied in Paris and Brussels and claimed by the Symbolists as one of their own. The Frenchmen who admire him have never seen a Morris and Company window in an English parish church.
suggested_refs: Laus Veneris (1873-1878), Laing Art Gallery, Newcastle; A. C. Swinburne's poem of the same title

stops.name: Rottingdean, Prospect House on the green
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1880; no month is given. The coordinate is corrected: the research pool's Rottingdean pins carried an eastward drift of roughly 400 m, placing them off the green and toward the seafront.
stops.campa: He buys Prospect House on the green at Rottingdean, a flint village in the chalk downs east of Brighton with the sea at the bottom of the street, and keeps it for eighteen years. The parish church on the green is St Margaret's. He will give it windows, have his ashes buried in its churchyard, and draw his nephew by marriage, Rudyard Kipling, to a house on the same green in the last year of his life. A second house on the green is joined to it later, and the pair goes by the name North End House.
suggested_refs: Prospect House and North End House on Rottingdean village green

stops.name: The Grange, The Golden Stairs
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1880 as the year of the painting; no month is given, and the pin is the studio where the work was made rather than a gallery.
stops.campa: He paints The Golden Stairs: eighteen women in pale robes descending a spiral stair, carrying instruments, going nowhere the picture discloses. Several of the faces are borrowed from his own household and from the daughters of friends, among them his daughter Margaret. The picture illustrates nothing: there is no text behind it and no saint in it, and a viewer who wants the story is given the arrangement instead. The Aesthetic Movement takes it for an emblem.
suggested_refs: The Golden Stairs (1880), Tate

stops.name: Exeter College, Oxford, the honorary fellow
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1881 (honorary degree) and 1882 (Honorary Fellow); the stop is pinned at the later year and no months are given. The pin is inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json's Exeter College stop.
stops.campa: Oxford, which he left in 1856 without a degree and without orders, gives him an honorary degree in 1881 and makes him an Honorary Fellow in 1882. He returns to the university as a man it now names, twenty-six years after walking out of it to be a painter in London on no income. The Union murals he helped paint in 1857 are by this time faded almost to nothing on the debating-hall wall a few streets away, and nobody proposes to restore them. His windows are in the college chapels all around, made by a firm and installed by workmen.
suggested_refs: The Honorary Fellowship of Exeter College, Oxford, conferred 1882

stops.name: Grosvenor Gallery, King Cophetua and the Beggar Maid
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1884 as the year of the painting and its acclaimed exhibition; no month is given, so the day defaults.
stops.campa: He paints King Cophetua and the Beggar Maid, out of the ballad by way of Tennyson: a king who has never desired a woman lays down his crown at the feet of a barefoot girl in grey and sits below her on the step, in armour, in a narrow gold room. She holds anemones and looks past him, and two boys sing from a gallery over their heads. Tennyson's poem on the subject is forty years old when he paints it. The picture is shown to great acclaim. It is the last of his works to be received without argument.

stops.name: Merton Abbey Works, the Adoration and the Holy Grail
stops.date_confidence: date and pin inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json, stop 'The tapestry loom, the Adoration and the Holy Grail'; the tapestry work spans years either side of this date.
stops.campa: At the Merton Abbey works on the river Wandle, where Morris has moved the dyeing and the looms, Burne-Jones supplies the cartoons for the high-warp tapestries: the Adoration of the Magi for an Oxford chapel, and the Quest of the Holy Grail. He draws the figures; Morris and John Henry Dearle fill in the foregrounds, the acanthus, the millefleurs. The Grail he first met in Malory at Oxford comes back at fifty-seven as wool on a loom, and the Lancelot who fails at the chapel door is his design.

stops.name: London, the second Briar Rose exhibited alone
stops.date_confidence: 1890 is attested for the exhibition of the second series by itself; no month or venue coordinate is given in the sources consulted, and the pin is an Old Bond Street approximation for the West End dealers' rooms.
stops.campa: The second Legend of the Briar Rose series is exhibited by itself: four long panels of a court asleep, the king among his councillors, the knights tangled in the thorn, the women at the loom, and the princess. Nobody in the pictures is awake and the prince has not arrived. He has been at the subject since the 1870s. The paintings are bought for Buscot Park and set into one room with a connecting frieze, so that the sleep runs unbroken round the walls of a house where people go on living.

stops.name: Birmingham, The Star of Bethlehem exhibited
stops.date_confidence: 1891 is attested for the exhibition, the painting having been worked 1887-91. The research pool placed it in 1890 alongside the Briar Rose; the verification pass split the two, and this file follows the split.
stops.campa: The Star of Bethlehem is exhibited, a watercolour of enormous size painted over four years for the corporation of Birmingham: the kings kneeling in a wooden shed, an angel standing among them holding the star like a lamp on a stalk, the Virgin under the thatch. It is made from a tapestry cartoon and it goes home to the town he was born in, where he has been president of the Society of Artists since 1885. He is fifty-eight. Georgiana is already keeping the notes that will become the Memorials.

stops.name: Burlington House, the resignation from the Royal Academy
stops.date_confidence: 1893 is attested for the formal resignation and November 1893 for the approach about a baronetcy; no month is given for the resignation itself, so the day defaults. The 1891 election to the Art Workers' Guild, carried in this stop's narrative, is attested to the year only.
stops.campa: Two years after being elected to the Art Workers' Guild, the society of designers and craftsmen that refuses the line between the fine arts and the trades, he formally resigns his Associateship of the Royal Academy. He was elected to it in 1885 and exhibited there once. His work leaves a Fulham garden studio for parish churches by way of a manufacturing firm, and reaches Burlington House only when he sends it there. In November of the same year he is approached about accepting a baronetcy. He does not refuse it.

stops.name: St Margaret's, Rottingdean, the three archangels
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1893 as the year of installation; no month is given. The coordinate is corrected from the research pool's value, which sat roughly 400 m east-southeast of the church.
stops.campa: Three lancet windows go into the east wall of St Margaret's, Rottingdean, designed by Burne-Jones and made by Morris and Company: Gabriel, Michael and Raphael, each standing full length in a narrow light. They are put in to commemorate the marriage of his daughter Margaret, born at Kensington Square twenty-seven years before. They are a father's wedding present in glass, and they stand five years before his ashes are buried a few yards outside the wall they light.

stops.name: The Grange, the hyphen and the baronetcy
stops.date_confidence: attested: the deed of name change in February 1894 and the creation of the baronetcy on 3 May 1894. The stop is pinned at the later, dated event.
stops.campa: In February he changes his surname by law to Burne-Jones, fixing with a hyphen the compound he has been signing for forty years; the Birmingham frame-maker's son Jones is retired by deed. On the third of May he is created a baronet, of Rottingdean in the county of Sussex and of the Grange in Fulham. The patent names two houses, the holiday village and the working studio, and no third place; Birmingham does not appear in it. Three years later Belgium elects him to its Royal Academy.
suggested_refs: The 1894 patent of baronetcy, 'of Rottingdean in the County of Sussex and of the Grange, Fulham'

stops.name: Upper Mall, Hammersmith, the Kelmscott Chaucer
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1896; no month is given in the pool, so the month here is arbitrary. The coordinate is corrected: the pool's value lay some 800 m east, near Furnivall Gardens, while the press stood at No. 14 Upper Mall beside Kelmscott House.
stops.campa: At 14 Upper Mall in Hammersmith, a few doors from Kelmscott House, Morris's press finishes the Chaucer: 425 paper copies at twenty pounds and thirteen on vellum at 120 guineas, with eighty-seven wood engravings after Burne-Jones set into Morris's borders and type. He leaves the coarse tales unillustrated and keeps comic situations out of the rest. Yeats calls it the most beautiful book of the age. The edition loses money and is carried by the press's other titles. It is the last work the two men make together.
stops.quote: pictures are too good to be funny
stops.quote_source: Burne-Jones's stated reason for omitting Chaucer's base stories and comic situations, reported in Wikipedia, 'Kelmscott Chaucer'

stops.name: St Philip's, Birmingham, the west window
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1897 as the year of dedication; no month is given. The subjects of the three eastern windows are a stated gap: the source consulted is silent on them and nothing here is inferred.
stops.campa: He designs the west window of St Philip's, Birmingham, dedicated this year in memory of Henry Bowlby, and three further windows at the east end of the same church. He was born and baptised a few streets away, near Bennett's Hill, in a frame-maker's house. The town that trained him at fifteen in a school of design built for its trades takes his glass at sixty-four and puts it in the church at the top of the hill. Whether he stood in the church and saw the glass lit is not recorded. In 1940 the building will be bombed, and the glass will already have been taken out and hidden.

stops.name: The Grange, the king still asleep
stops.date_confidence: 1898 is attested as the year of the unfinished work, pursued since around 1881; no month is given, so the day defaults.
stops.campa: On the great easel in the Fulham studio stands The Last Sleep of Arthur in Avalon, begun around 1881 and never finished: the king asleep on a bier under a canopy, queens watching, hills behind, the whole thing more than twenty feet wide. He works at it in his last months. Malory, found at Oxford in his twenties, is where the picture comes from, and the Grail tapestries and the Union murals came from the same book. He dies with the king still asleep and the canvas still open.
suggested_refs: The Last Sleep of Arthur in Avalon (c. 1881-1898), Museo de Arte de Ponce

stops.name: The Grange, North End, Fulham, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The coordinate is corrected: the research pool pinned the death at 51.5074, -0.1278, the generic Charing Cross pin for London, about 6.5 km east of the Grange.
stops.campa: Influenza takes him in the spring and he seems to recover. On the night of the sixteenth of June he collapses a second time, at the Grange in North End, Fulham, and dies there in the early hours of the seventeenth, aged sixty-four. Georgiana is in the house. The studio behind him holds the unfinished Avalon, the Briar Rose cartoons, and thirty-one years of work; the parish churches of England hold several thousand of his figures in glass, most of them signed by a firm and not by a man.
suggested_refs: The Grange, North End, Fulham, and the studio as it stood in June 1898

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the memorial service
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, six days after the death. The claim that it was the first such honour for an artist is the source's own wording and is not independently checked here.
stops.campa: Six days after the death a memorial service is held for him in Westminster Abbey, at the intervention of the Prince of Wales. Sources record it as the first time an artist had been so honoured there. The body is not in the building. Kings, poets and generals lie under this floor, and a Birmingham frame-maker's son who left Oxford without a degree is read over among them, forty-two years after he gave up the idea of taking orders. His ashes go afterwards to a village churchyard in Sussex.
suggested_refs: The memorial service of 23 June 1898, Westminster Abbey

stops.name: St Margaret's, Rottingdean, the ashes on the green
stops.date_confidence: 1898 is attested for the interment; no date within the year is given, so the month here is arbitrary. The coordinate is the corrected church position, replacing the research pool's value some 400 m to the east-southeast.
stops.campa: His ashes are buried in the churchyard of St Margaret's on the green at Rottingdean, under the three archangel windows he gave the church five years earlier for his daughter's wedding. Georgiana's ashes will join his, and so will those of their granddaughter, the novelist Angela Thirkell. On the same green stands The Elms, where Rudyard Kipling, his nephew by marriage, came to live the year before and wrote much of the Just So Stories. Kipling's house and the churchyard face each other across the same grass.

stops.name: Tate Gallery, Millbank, the centenary nobody came to
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the opening; the 1973 monograph and 1975 biography named in the campa are attested by year only.
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of June, a hundred years after the birth, his nephew Stanley Baldwin, Prime Minister, opens an exhibition of the drawings and paintings at the Tate Gallery on Millbank. It is recorded as poorly attended. Between the wars the Victorians are a joke with a beard on it, and the pictures come out of store into a room with nobody in it. Forty years pass before Martin Harrison and Bill Waters publish their monograph in 1973 and Penelope Fitzgerald her biography in 1975, and the pictures begin to be looked at again.

stops.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, the centenary of the death
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1998; no month is given. stops.campa: A century after the death, the centenary retrospective opens not in London but at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, and travels on to Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery and then to the Musee d'Orsay in Paris. No London museum is a venue on the tour. Birmingham holds the largest collection in the world; Paris holds the Symbolists who took him for a founder and whom he never joined.
